Another trick: laying belts around the luggage perimeter so that they’re easier to find.

To keep things condensed and organized, McAlpin suggests compression cubes. These small bags feature two zippers: a main zipper that closes the cube like a standard bag, and a second perimeter zipper that pulls the cube’s top and bottom panels closer together, squeezing out excess air and reducing volume. Compression cubes help eliminate air pockets that come with traditional folding and can reduce the volume of soft clothes like T-shirts and pants up to 30 percent.

Another option: roll-up compression bags. These pump-free, vacuum-free storage bags use one-way pressure valves to push air out, cutting volume by up to 80 percent. “I use these for laundry,” claims McAlpin, because they temporarily block odors.

“They’re like an industrial Ziploc bag,” she says, and great for bulky items like a fleece jacket. But use them sparingly. Roll sacks are typically made of plastic and cause a lot more wrinkles than traditional compression cubes.

McAlpin carries dry laundry sheets and a two-gallon Ziploc bag for washing clothes. “The bag doesn’t take up any room, and then I can wash my socks and underwear without worrying if I’ve left any toothpaste in the sink.”.

Recent findings suggest that mcAlpin notes her packing “3:1 ratio” (three tops to every bottom) has “changed people’s lives.” She packs nine tops and three bottoms, and everything mixes and matches. “I base everything around two colors,” she says, “like a black and a tan,” and then throws in an occasional splash of color.

Recent findings suggest that this works, notes McAlpin, because human memory registers outfits based on what’s closest to the head and face. And while she travels with three pairs of shoes, each one should be for something different. For example, runners for long walks, sandals for the beach, and loafers for evenings.

Sources indicate that as for the bag itself, McAlpin notes four-wheel bags (spinner luggage) are a must. Not only are they easy to maneuver through packed terminals and airplane aisles, the ability to push the bag upright beside you keeps your arm in a neutral, bent-elbow position. This places less stress on your wrists, shoulders, and lower back compared to pulling a two-wheel bag behind you, and plays a substantial role in easing ergonomic strain.

Recent findings suggest that they’re also ideal for stacking, since they stay upright. Think about it, indicates McAlpin. “When you pack your heavy tote bag on top of your suitcase, it’s the bag, not your shoulders, that’s carrying the weight.”.

Ultimately, the idea is to make use of all your space, keep items from bumping around inside your suitcase and (if possible) wrinkle-free, and to not throw out your back in the process.

Of course, when it comes to finding room for souvenirs, there’s always the Mary Poppins packing method. But after talking with McAlpin, I’ve been using her method exclusively. My clothes, formerly creased, rumpled, and crinkled, are now decidedly wrinkle-free!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%. And now, you can buy one.

Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

Sources indicate that “The (Tadano) V320RC marks a real breakthrough in the pick & carry industry,” reads the official Tadano launch copy. “Rather than an evolution of existing solutions, it introduces a new philosophy, with technologies and features capable of setting new benchmarks in the lifting market. Tadano and NMG Italia continue their collaboration in the field, turning real-world experience into new technological solutions to meet the most advanced demands of industrial lifting.”.

The crane itself is a compact, battery-electric pick-and-carry machine with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Measuring just 5 m long, 2.15 m wide and 2.400 m tall (a meter is about a yard, guys – you got this), the V320RC is designed to bring heavy lifting capability into tight industrial spaces where larger cranes struggle to operate.

The newly introduced Tadano runs on a 120V, 1,120 Ah li-ion battery pack (that works out to ~134 kWh) and packs a gross vehicle weight of more than 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tones). That number includes 9,500 kg (~10 tons) of removable counterweights that make transport and handling easier for a wider range of customers. Under the hood, a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with what the company calls “an electro-hydraulic control valve” to improve precision and responsiveness while reducing energy consumption.

According to NMG Italia, all that baked-in tech V320RC give them 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes working under equivalent workloads, with enough battery capacity to support several days of operation between charges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A Jeep® Brand vehicle exploring the wilderness has always been accompanied by a particular soundtrack. As it powers forward along a rutted trail or works its way over an obstacle, you hear the rumble of the motor, the growl of the exhaust, and the confident chatter of the four-wheel drivetrain. It’s the collective refrain of a highly capable machine, all its parts working, quite literally, in concert, to accomplish something difficult.

The all-upcoming, all-electric Jeep® Recon changes the score. There is still the sensation of commanding a legendary Trail Rated® off-road vehicle, proficient at maneuvering toward destinations far beyond where the pavement ends. But, without the mechanical thrum of an internal combustion engine and multi-speed transmission, what you hear now, with enhanced precision, is what this immensely capable SUV is doing. The massive knobby tires gaining grip, the underbody protection pinging against the landscape, or your spotter delivering precise instructions.

More than this, in the all-electric Jeep® Recon, you hear the whole vast symphony of the natural world around you—the wind blowing, the animals and insects calling, the plants and trees rustling—immersing you further in the experience of being in nature, of getting away from it all.

Recent findings suggest that with as much as 670 horsepower and 620 pound-feet of torque, the Jeep® Recon represents one of the more radical interpretations of the brand’s venerable 4x4 philosophy. Capable of hustling from 0-60 mph in just 3.6 seconds,¹ it can blow the doors off just about anything on the road, or off. Including, amusingly enough, itself. Like the brand's most iconic 4x4s, the Jeep® Recon features fully removable doors, honoring the brand’s legendary commitment to true open-air freedom.

Unlike other electric SUVs, which borrow the visual language of adventure while spending most of their lives commuting between the office and charging stations, the Jeep® Recon derives proudly from an unwavering heritage of off-road capability and is the only fully electric vehicle to earn the Trail Rated® badge.

Recent findings suggest that this trademarked emblem isn't decorative. It’s a medal of honor. Vehicles stamped with this designation are subjected to rigorous and brutal testing in five core areas: traction, water fording, maneuverability, articulation, and ground clearance. The Jeep® Recon attained that status for good reason, because it was designed from the outset for adventure. The electric powertrain is an outgrowth of its core mission, which is, first and foremost, to be a great Jeep Brand vehicle.

According to recent reports, the result is not simply an accomplished off-roader that happens to run on electrons. It’s a real world, pavement-ripping, mountain-climbing demonstration of what happens when electrification is integrated fully into the brand’s off-road DNA.

Electric propulsion has obvious advantages when playing in the mud, sand, gravel, or snow. Peak torque arrives as soon as you get on the accelerator. This means that there is no need to wait for an engine to build revs, and no need to downshift to find the right gear or the right part of the powerband. For an off roader, that characteristic can be very significant in the steep, deep, and technical portions of an adventure, providing the capability to throttle up an incline, over difficult terrain, and through the water.

To control all that twist—all 620 pound-feet of it—in whatever difficult situation you find or place yourself, the Jeep® Recon’s four-wheel drive is paired, as standard equipment, with the brand’s patented Selec-Terrain® traction management system. This setup provides the driver with five selectable modes, each of which controls the throttle mapping as well as the output of both the front and rear electric motors. This configuration allows precise torque distribution and delivery, keyed to different circumstances, maximizing the vehicle’s ability to grip, slip, thrust, and crawl through various surfaces and conditions.

In Snow mode, the system diminishes the onset of initial torque in order to prevent tire slip. In Sand, it allows controlled wheel spin, so that you can avoid bogging down deeper into the dunes. In Rock mode, it optimizes torque distribution and enhances the accelerator’s precision to allow the Jeep® Recon to crawl slowly and carefully over uneven, rugged terrain. And in Auto, it seeks the perfect balance between potency and efficiency, for those rare times when you find yourself on regular paved roads.

Finally, there’s Sport mode. If you toggle into this setting, the system sharpens tip-in and throttle response in order to maximize accelerative capacity, unleashing the kind of instant torque you’d expect from a performance-driven electric vehicle like the Jeep® Recon. The sheer performance numbers are astounding for almost any vehicle category, but especially for a mid-size SUV. Zero to 60 mph arrives in 3.6 seconds. Numbers like these are typically associated with sports cars, not rugged, all-terrain vehicles designed to ford streams.

It has been revealed that in fact, that’s kind of the point. The Jeep® Recon doesn't ask you to choose between performance and capability. Its novel electric architecture lets you have both. On a wide country road, with the doors removed and the canvas roof powered back, 670 horsepower make the Jeep® Recon a startling way to cut loose. On loose terrain, instant torque and electronically managed traction become tools for maintaining control.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge was to preserve the essence of a rugged Trail Rated® 4x4, while radically changing the system that powers it. It has succeeded. The all-electric Jeep® Recon doesn’t discard conventional notions of adventure. It redefines them.

It’s very clear, even at first glance, that the newly introduced Jeep® Recon is designed for adventure. The shape reads unmistakably as a Jeep Brand vehicle. The traditional seven-slot grille stands sentinel up front, like a line of climbers about to conquer a rock face. The short front and rear overhangs provide clues to its capacity to get in and out of challenging situations. The expansive greenhouse offers 360-degree visibility, providing straight sightlines to all four corners of the vehicle, so you can always see what kind of trouble you’re approaching or departing. The design, unapologetically squared-off but just rounded and flush fitted enough to nod to aerodynamic efficiency, is heritage-inspired without being nostalgic.

More importantly, the Jeep® Recon is designed to let you interact directly with whatever landscape you’re traversing, to let the outside in. All four doors can be removed, without tools, using quick-release hardware. The back quarter windows and rear glass can be readily popped off and stored in the cargo hatch. The available Sky One-Touch® Power Top can retract fully at the touch of a button.

According to recent reports, all this openness means that any boundaries between the cabin and the trail are greatly diminished. The sun and the wind around you, the vistas above, and the scents and sounds of the terrain below all become part of the drive. On a forest road, a desert wash, or a mountain pass, you can look up and out in every direction, privileging your vital centrality in your own adventure.

The interior of an off-road vehicle has to function as a command center. The Jeep® Recon acknowledges that reality. The materials are rugged and hard-wearing, thoughtfully assembled to withstand spirited four-season go-anywhere outdoor use. The switchgear comes to hand readily, whether your hands are covered in ice-climbing gloves or rock-climbing chalk. The technology functions in support of your missions but retreats from your sightlines when its presence isn’t required.

Recent findings suggest that your adventure gear should also uplift and coddle you. To this end, the Jeep® Recon’s cabin is highly refined and thoughtfully designed. Quality handcrafted materials abound, with anodized switchgear, knurled knobs, and richly patterned perforated seating surfaces, the latter of which feature available heating in all four outboard positions as well as cooling in the front two spots. Clever well-integrated storage bins are plentiful, including a lockable one between the seats—handy in an SUV designed to explore the world without the protection of windows and doors. Elastic straps keep your water bottles from rattling in, or out of, the door pockets. Speakers for the booming sound system are mounted under the seats, ensuring you don’t lose your tunes when you remove the doors. And because it’s an EV, without an engine up front, there’s a clever storage space under the hood, perfect for holding your compressor, tools, or blender.

Industry observers note that the infotainment system exists to serve your needs. The centerpiece is a 14.5-inch touchscreen, the largest touchscreen the Jeep Brand offers in any of its vehicles.² This is paired with a 12.3-inch digital cluster display. Four USB ports and a wireless charging pad keep your phone and headphones juiced up, and an available onboard Wi-Fi hotspot provides connectivity when you’re out of range. And a 115-volt outlet adds the sort of utility that becomes surprisingly valuable when camping in the backcountry.

The Jeep® Recon’s custom EV architecture was designed intentionally to feel intuitive and functional, whether you’re commuting to work on-road, or escaping from it off-road. Powered by a high-capacity battery built for endurance, it offers the ability to fast-charge from 5 to 80 percent in about 28 minutes. And regardless of whether your route is planned or unplanned, the Uconnect infotainment system can help you find nearby compatible charging stations, so you’ll always be ready for your next adventure.

According to recent reports, the Recon never forgets that driving a Jeep® Brand vehicle is supposed to bring joy. To support this initiative, it sports a pair of 335-hp electric motors, one in front and one in back, providing a combined 670-hp. That’s enough to launch this rugged machine from 0-60 in 3.6 seconds.

In a recent development, electrification has its practical applications off-road as well. It can thrust the Recon through its 24” fording depth. It can help you get into the rough, making use of its 9.1-inches of ground clearance, its 33.8-degree approach angle, 33.1-degree departure angle, and 23.3-degree breakover angle. And it can apply power to each wheel in very precise increments, allowing the Recon to crawl up difficult terrain with bravado and technical sophistication. The brand’s Trail Rated objectives remain the same, but the Recon occupies a more unusual space, because it’s a Jeep® Brand vehicle first, and an electric vehicle second. It has the visual confidence you expect from the nameplate. It has the Trail Rated 4X4 capability. It has removable doors and windows, and a power roof that can disappear at the push of a button, providing a liberating open-air architecture. It has the technology expected of a modern SUV and enough interior flexibility to function as a daily driver. And, don’t forget, it has 650-hp.

In a recent development, the Recon’s electrification makes it faster, quieter, more controllable, and more exciting. Yet the core Jeep® Brand mission hasn't changed. That's key to the brand’s enduring appeal, and it’s why the 2026 Recon matters. Despite packing a state-of-the-art tech suite that includes a next-gen EV platform, a 14.5-inch touchscreen display, and an advanced Selec-Terrain system that enables an astonishing 3.6-second sprint to 60 mph, the vehicle's greatest achievement isn't digital. It’s the fact that underneath the silicon and cells, the core philosophy remains wonderfully old-fashioned. Adventure should take you somewhere.

Thanks and Giving, a Recipe for a Happy Life

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday, a sentiment I frequently hear from others.
  • Recent findings suggest that unlike other holidays, there are no gifts to buy or exchange, no decorations to hang, or costumes to wear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

Thanksgiving has always been my favorite holiday, a sentiment I frequently hear from others.

What makes Thanksgiving so beloved? Its simplicity, I think.

Recent findings suggest that unlike other holidays, there are no gifts to buy or exchange, no decorations to hang, or costumes to wear. Instead, we gather, connect, give thanks, and eat. Across religious beliefs and family traditions, this day offers an opportunity to sit around a table, prepare and share a meal, and appreciate what is present in our lives.

Of course, Thanksgiving holds different meanings and histories for different people. It can also bring grief, loneliness, and family tension. Yet, I wonder whether the enduring appeal reveals something key about our psychological needs and the path to a well-lived life.

Sources indicate that the word thanksgiving dates back to the 1530s, when it referred to the act of expressing gratitude. By the 1600s, it became associated with public celebrations of thanks, and later became the American holiday we know today.

Beyond the delicious meal, I believe Thanksgiving offers a recipe for living. The word itself implies action. Thanks is how we appreciate life, and giving is how we participate in it. By giving, we move our gratitude into service. Gratitude changes what we notice, while giving changes what we do with what we notice. Together, they create a powerful practice of recognizing and reciprocating the goodness in our lives.

I think of Thanks+Giving as a prescription in perception, a conscious practice for approaching life with greater grace, generosity, and connection.

Recent findings suggest that in my clinical work and my own life, I see how expectations contribute to emotional suffering. Often, we become attached to how people should behave or feel, how circumstances should unfold, or how life should look. Gratitude offers another perspective. It encourages curiosity and appreciation, even when things are not as expected.

Research increasingly supports the psychological benefits of gratitude. An international study with over 10,000 participants found that even brief gratitude practices produced modest improvements in positive mood and well-being (Coles et al., 2026). In another recent study with 1,240 participants, researchers found that expressing gratitude in supportive relationships improved both emotional well-being and relationship quality (Nelson-Coffey et al., 2026). Maybe the power of gratitude is how little it takes to experience the benefits.

My daily gratitude practice is a running list of three things I appreciate. Today, I added trees, my friend Josie, and apples. I do not add explanations or further descriptions. Naming something as ordinary as a tree leads me to notice it again and appreciate its qualities, without asking it to do or be more than it is. Children often find wonder in these ordinary gifts, something we can miss amid the responsibilities and distractions of adulthood.

Noticing our gratitude does not necessarily erase grief, disappointment, or longing. We can think of gratitude as expanding our emotional experience, not denying what hurts. For example, we can miss someone while appreciating the moments we shared. We can be worried about tomorrow while finding something beautiful in today. Gratitude can co-exist with other emotions, and direct our momentary focus toward something positive.

I like to remind myself to look for the awe in all, rather than waiting for something extraordinary to call awesome.

If gratitude allows us to recognize goodness, giving suggests we share it. Giving is both an expression and an extension of gratitude.

Recent findings suggest that another 2026 study examined whether “grateful” people were more likely to engage in generous acts. Drawing on large international samples and field research, the researchers found that people with a disposition toward gratitude were more likely to engage in personally costly actions benefiting others (Lee et al., 2026). Interestingly, temporarily inducing gratitude did not produce the same effect. This suggests that an enduring grateful orientation is more closely associated with generosity than a fleeting moment of appreciation.

Industry observers note that we usually think of generosity in terms of money, donations, or charitable work. But giving can also mean attention, compassion, encouragement, time, and presence of mind for both others and ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that again, simplicity might hold the secret. I remember my daughter, as a young child, finding a tiny flower, and immediately gifting it to me, my husband, or her brother. She found something that inspired awe and without hesitation, she passed it on.

Sources indicate that that spontaneous gesture captures the beautiful reciprocity of giving. Without expecting anything in return, we can experience true connection and the satisfaction of contributing to another person’s joy. The recipient receives a gift, and the giver experiences the pleasure of sharing something meaningful.

This giving can also include ourselves. Resting when we are tired, accepting help, and treating ourselves with kindness and care, are forms of generosity that sustain our capacity to give to others.

It has been revealed that beyond our annual Thanksgiving feast, what if we made time for thanks and giving every day? Imagine pausing throughout the day to ask ourselves two simple questions:.

What can I name that I am grateful for in this moment?

What can I consciously give to myself or others in this moment?

The answers and actions do not need to be grand. The recipe is remarkably simple: Notice something good. Give something good. Repeat.

In a recent development, when we make Thanks+Giving a daily practice, we may discover that the joys of living emerge where gratitude, connection, and service meet. It may just be that the secret sauce to a happy life is found in the name of a favorite holiday.

Latest Update: This EV-Swapped 1967 Porsche 912 Has 300 HP And A Split Battery Pack

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world.
  • It has been revealed that according to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving.
  • Sources indicate that there's some clever engineering here, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world. It started out doing electric powertrain swaps for classic Range Rovers, which it still does. But it also has a bespoke program now, under which it will develop custom EV swaps for customers for any sort of car they want. In this specific case, Inverted stuffed some batteries and an electric motor into an old Porsche 912. Interestingly, this is the third powertrain that's been in this Porsche.

It has been revealed that according to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving. So they took their car to Inverted and the team got to work. The end result is a car that looks exactly like a normal Porsche 912, with all of its gorgeous old-school styling, but drives like a modern EV.

Sources indicate that there's some clever engineering here, too. The 62 kWh battery pack is more than enough to propel the vintage Porsche's featherweight body a fair ways. However, that's a lot of weight to hang over the rear axle. Air-cooled Porsches were already prone to lift-off oversteer, so they don't need any more. So Inverted came up with an interesting solution: split the pack into two parts. On section is mounted out back where the engine used to be, and the other is under the hood. It means the electric 912's weight balance is actually better than the original car's.

Sources indicate that inverted claims that this EV 912 has around 250 miles of range, and it can DC fast charge at 75 kW. The latter might seem weak in the world of modern EVs, but it's perfectly fine in a classic like this. This is a daily driver, not a long-distance cruiser. So 250 miles is more than enough for daily usage, and plugging it in overnight to charge will get the owner a fresh battery in the morning.

It has been revealed that the rear-mounted electric motor makes 300 horsepower, so it's much more potent than the original 912 four-cylinder engine which made around 90 horsepower. Inverted says it can hit 0-60 mph in four seconds, which kicks the ass of the stock vehicle. The original 912 took about 13 seconds.

According to recent reports, this isn't just a powertrain swap, either. Its interior is completely redone and it's gorgeous. The gauges look like vintage Porsche gauges but they're modified for EV used. For example, the classic Porsche central tachometer was replaced with a power percentage gauge. The fuel gauge is now an analog battery charge gauge, too. It's just lovely.

Industry observers note that this is an awesome project and one that would make for an incredible daily driver. It has modern Porsche levels of performance, with modern EV levels of range, in a stylish vintage package. Seems perfect.

#86610. Latest Update: How a red wolf gets a checkup

Latest Update: How a red wolf gets a checkup

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (363 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that annual human checkups are relatively straightforward.
  • We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam.
  • “The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that annual human checkups are relatively straightforward. You hop onto the exam table, stick your tongue out, stare straight ahead as the doctor beams light into your eyes, let them tap their small hammer against that wildly uncomfortable spot under your kneecap, etc. But for wildlife, it’s a whole other experience.

We’ve previously discovered that conducting a checkup on a 140 pound stingray takes eight people, that you can weigh an octopus with a laundry basket, and that bears should always be under anesthesia before their exam. But what about another favorite carnivore—wolves? According to Vicki Scharfberg, from Roger Williams Park Zoo & Carousel Village in Rhode Island, the annual wellness examination for red wolves (Canis rufus) is not that different from a pet dog’s annual veterinary visit.

“The biggest difference is the level of restraint or sedation needed for red wolves, since they are wild animals and not habituated to human contact,” she tells Popular Science.

The checkup includes a physical examination at the wolf enclosure or the zoo veterinary hospital, bloodwork, vaccinations, heartworm prevention care, and if necessary, parasite treatment. A social media post by Roger Williams Park Zoo showcases their red wolf named Frye thoroughly knocked out on the exam table, undergoing an oral exam, among other things.

The team uses the bloodwork to check on the wolf’s organs and screen for heartworm disease. Interestingly, their vaccines are the exact same ones veterinarians give to domestic dogs for rabies, distemper, parvovirus, and leptospirosis.

Heartworm prevention treatment involves a long-acting 12 month injection. Heartworm disease is caused by grossly long worms called heartworms that take up residence in an animals’ heart, lungs, and related blood vessels. This parasitic condition triggers severe lung disease, heart failure, and damages other organs. Heartworm is potentially fatal, and in addition to wolves can also impact animals including dogs, cats, ferrets, foxes, and humans.

“If something abnormal is found on the examination, we follow up with additional diagnostics like x-rays, ultrasound, or a consult with a veterinary specialist (dentist, cardiologist, etc),” Scharfberg concludes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

According to recent reports, ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Industry observers note that speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Sources indicate that then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the newly introduced regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of upcoming careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

In a recent development, the aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

It has been revealed that in November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing latest free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

Industry observers note that while you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free patch, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Illinois Clean Ports Program is putting $104 million behind efforts to help clean up its working waterfronts, funds earmarked for heavy-duty electric equipment assets that includes forklifts, giant reach stackers, switcher locomotives, and the charging equipment needed to support them. There’s even a passenger ferry!

In a recent development, procurement is now underway for zero-emission vehicles, equipment, and supporting infrastructure at four sites across the state. Administered by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (Illinois EPA), Illinois’ Clean Ports Program aims to modernize operations at ports and waterfront facilities in Chicago, the Quad Cities, and southern Illinois’ river port districts.

Recent findings suggest that “Illinois’ waterways are a competitive advantage for the state,” said Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, who was elected to a historic third term on 03NOV. “By modernizing port infrastructure, advancing zero-emission technology, and improving air quality, we are strengthening our economy while building a cleaner future for Illinois.”.

Illinois’ Clean Ports Program isn’t just replacing diesel-powered equipment with electric alternatives – instead, the proposal also includes Level 2 and DC fast charging, shore power and charging for electrified ships, and comprehensive grid upgrades designed to modernize existing port operations and support the deployment of new electric equipment.

Sources indicate that the program takes a holistic approach to port electrification at Chicago’s Illinois International Port District (IIPD), treating energy generation, storage, and deployment as parts of a single connected system. On-site solar helps meet the port’s growing electricity needs while excess power is stored for peak hours, when grid electricity is most expensive. This setup reduces strain on the local grid, and acts as a hedge against rising energy costs.

According to recent reports, for smaller public port districts, replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be an enormous financial undertaking. The Illinois Clean Ports Program helps make those investments possible, bringing cleaner, healthier, zero-emission technology within reach of terminal operators while preparing the state’s ports for a more competitive freight future.

#86606. How to Move From Worrisome What-Ifs to Wondering What-Ifs

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (545 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

How to Move From Worrisome What-Ifs to Wondering What-Ifs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • If you're tired of feeling like you're never quite enough, or that you're never going to get "there" (wherever there is), consider the following questions.
  • Instead of skimming through these questions the way you might read a typical blog post, I'd like to suggest that you wait until you have a quiet moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

If you're tired of feeling like you're never quite enough, or that you're never going to get "there" (wherever there is), consider the following questions.

Instead of skimming through these questions the way you might read a typical blog post, I'd like to suggest that you wait until you have a quiet moment. Sit or lie down. Read the words silently or out loud, and really consider them. Try them on, the way you might try on a piece of clothing to see how they fit.

In a recent development, notice what happens inside your body as you read. See if any of these ideas can sink in. If they can't right now, that's OK, too.

Sometimes old programming runs deep and can feel hard to change. With patience and practice, old beliefs can be questioned and updated, and new ways of thinking and being can take root.

So get comfortable, take a slow, deep breath, and consider these possibilities.

What if I remembered that self-critical thoughts aren't necessarily facts, and I didn't have to believe everything I think?

What if I could begin choosing fresh thoughts and beliefs that are kinder, more supportive, and actually feel good?

What if I got off my own back, got on my own side, and decided that I am a good person doing the best I can?

What if I remembered that kindness, compassion, and encouragement help people grow, while berating, pressure, and perfectionism often get in the way?

What if my worth didn't depend on how much I accomplished, how productive I was, or how well I did things?

What if I allowed myself to do things imperfectly, and let good enough be good enough?

What if I could let myself be a beginner, make mistakes, change my mind, and learn as I go, rather than expecting myself to get everything right every time?

What if I spent less time living in worst-case scenarios about the future and more time in the present moment?

What if I slowed down, ever so slightly, and sprinkled small moments of conscious breathing and quiet awareness throughout my day?

What if I stepped out of the never-ending race to get somewhere and spent more moments in actual, factual reality?

What if I softened my gaze when I looked at myself and softened my thoughts when I thought about myself?

What if I spent less time comparing myself to others, remembering that I know nothing about what their lives actually feel like on the inside, and instead offered myself more moments of grace?

What if I became curious about what enoughness feels like?

What if I decided that, in this exact moment, I am already enough? I can still do what I'm moved to do, pursue what matters to me, and take care of what needs to be done without staying trapped on the endless treadmill of never-enoughness.

What if I simply stated, Thank you for what I have, kept the welcome mat out, and stayed open to whatever comes next?

What if, just for today, I let myself be enough?

#86605. Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (966 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Bears don’t sleep all winter, and other cold-weather animal myths

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (966 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • Industry observers note that that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter.
  • Many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s almost winter in the Northern Hemisphere. While the humans fire up their furnaces (or, ideally, heat pumps), animals prepare in their own ways.

Industry observers note that that brings to mind a number of misconceptions people have about animals in the winter. Most of us were taught things that, over time, were proven to be untrue, and winter behaviors are no exception. Bears, for example, don’t sleep the entire winter. Birds don’t actually care about the cold that much, and migrate for other reasons. And squirrels aren’t constantly forgetting the location of their nuts. Let’s dig into these common winter myths, and what actual research points to.

Many of us learned in school or on TV that bears sleep all winter. It’s not true—bears don’t hibernate. At least, not exactly.

An explainer published by the National Park Service states that hibernation isn’t a black-and-white concept: “In recent years the view that the state of hibernation exists on a spectrum rather than as a binary yes-or-no condition is becoming more entrenched.” The piece goes on to say that black bears don’t hibernate as deeply as smaller animals.

There’s real research backing this up. A 2011 study published in Science by researchers at the University of Alaska Fairbanks highlights that bears get up and shift position throughout the winter. “Animals changed position twice a day to once every 2 days, when they stood, occasionally groomed, and rearranged bedding material,” the study states. The research also states that bears use a great deal more energy during the winter than smaller animals. “During torpor, metabolic rates of small hibernators decrease to 2 to 5 percent of basal metabolic rate (BMR),” the study explains, before showing that bears’ metabolic rates reach closer to 25 percent. That’s a wide spectrum.

According to recent reports, so bears don’t sleep all winter—they regularly get up. That brings us to another myth: The idea that bears give birth without waking up. It’s also not true, according to the National Park Service.

“They’re not only awake during this time, but in the days before birthing, expectant mothers will often add bedding to the den by chewing materials into smaller pieces and arranging them just-so,” the explainer states. “After the 1 to 3 half-ounce to 1 lb cubs are born, she meticulously licks them clean, and provides warmth and mother’s milk as they grow to about 5 lbs by the time they emerge in spring.”.

Which isn’t to say that bears are active in winter—they really do slow down. But they don’t hibernate to the same extent as smaller animals.

Recent findings suggest that you might think that birds fly south for the winter because they don’t want to freeze—we even call cold-hating humans who travel in winter “snowbirds,” in reference to this belief. But it turns out birds aren’t directly concerned with cold weather.

Sources indicate that if you have a bird feeder you’ve probably noticed that many birds stick around for the winter.An explainer by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology states that birds are perfectly capable of surviving winter temperatures. “Escaping cold temperatures is not itself a major factor that drives birds to migrate, since many species, even hummingbirds, can withstand freezing temperatures as long as an adequate supply of food is available,” the article states.

Recent findings suggest that there’s less food around in the winter, and that’s the actual reason for migration. You might say this is semantics, and you’re not entirely wrong—the cold temperature causes the food shortage. But if you’re picturing shivering birds, desperate to travel somewhere warmer, you’re imagining the wrong motivation. Birds don’t leave in pursuit of warmer weather; they leave in pursuit of food and longer daylight hours. And they head back north (or south) in the spring for the same reason: the thaw means a lot of fresh food, not to mention safe, open areas for breeding.

Recent findings suggest that squirrels spend a good part of the year hiding nuts, all so they can recover them in the winter. A common legend goes something like this: squirrels forget about most of these nuts, and that’s how forests grow. And while it is true that squirrel caches can become trees, squirrels don’t forget their nuts that often.

Industry observers note that they are, in fact, really good at keeping track of their nuts, and this has been known for decades. A 1991 paper published in Animal Behaviour by researchers at Princeton University revealed this. In the study, captive grey squirrels were all given hazelnuts to bury in the same area. The nuts were then all removed by experimenters. The squirrels were re-introduced to the site, one by one, with a twist: experimenters buried fresh nuts in the squirrel’s own 10 cache sites and an equal number of sites randomly chosen from caches made by other squirrels.

Sources indicate that the results were striking. “Although each squirrel’s own caches were close to the caches of other squirrels, the squirrels retrieved significantly more nuts from their own sites than from sites used by other squirrels, after all delays,” the paper states. “The retrieval accuracy of the squirrels under these conditions indicates that while grey squirrels can locate buried nuts by their odour, they can also remember the individual locations of nuts they have buried.”.

Recent findings suggest that other studies show how well squirrels can remember nuts. A 2023 study published in Urban Ecosystems by researchers from Poland found that hazelnuts cached by squirrels are more likely to be dug up than hazelnuts buried by humans in the same area. This suggests that squirrels are pretty good at remembering where they buried their nuts.

Waymo Is Recalling Its Robotaxis Because They're Not Great At Dealing With Human Instructions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing issues with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections.
  • The tech giant's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents.
  • The robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing issues with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections. For anyone who has been following Waymo closely, this shouldn't be that surprising.

The tech giant's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents. Waymo took the voluntary step of suspending interstate operation nationwide on Wednesday, meaning the entire fleet is now back to running primarily on local roads and minor state highways.

The robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions. But the trouble seems to be when something unexpected pops up. Regulators from California cited poor behavior surrounding closed lanes and construction zones, a recurring issue for the organization, along with a another recent high-profile incident involving a California Highway Patrol rolling road block.

In a recent development, if you don't know what that last sentence means, you aren't alone. When I first moved to California a few years ago, I had no idea what a rolling road block or "traffic break" meant in normal parlance. But drive California freeways long enough and you'll experience one. A CHP cruiser or a group of them joins the highway, puts on its lights, and slowly zigzags across all lanes of traffic, blocking drivers from passing or exceeding the speed of the maneuver. The goal is typically to create a safe break in traffic for authorities to removed debris, clear and accident, or otherwise operate on the road. Sometimes it just slows down the herd before it barrels into a blind-corner accident scene at 80 mph.

In a recent development, when I first experienced this, I was plenty confused. But when I saw cops swerving in front of me with lights on, I naturally just slowed down and stayed behind me. Common sense told me that a cop swerving around with their lights on probably isn't looking for a race. Unfortunately, though, autonomous driving software doesn't always know how to interpret novel situations. So when a Waymo got caught behind a rolling road block, here's what it did:.

In a recent development, yep, it tried to blow right by. CHP was able to hold it back, but I've seen a Trooper controlling six lanes of traffic with one car before. Add in an inventive and disobedient robotaxi and you can see how it could create a dangerous situation wherein an autonomous vehicle is driving down a road that construction workers or police think is effectively closed.

Now, Waymos are good enough at avoiding hitting things that I don't expect this would have been too bad. But even a small chance of a runaway robotaxi is unacceptable to regulators and to Waymo, so it's good to pause freeway operations until they figure things out.

Industry observers note that but the road block situation is indicative of a larger matter with autonomous vehicles, and perhaps the most interesting one. We think of driving as a predominantly legal or process-driven endeavor. You stop at stop signs, obey the speed limit, and keep it between the lines. Errors happen, but we tend to see them as based on improperly applied rules.

Yet the police here are disrupting the rules and enforcing an unscheduled and ad-hoc temporary speed limit and traffic flow. If you're from out of state or haven't experienced it yet, it's confusing, as there's direct ruleset for an impromptu situation like that. Yet any other driver caught in this situation wouldn't blow past the cop car. Like me, they'd approach it cautiously, and let the police car take the lead.

Recent findings suggest that that is the matter I'm referring to: Driving is not just about rules and infrastructure. It's a social behavior. We wave each other ahead at stop signs and intersections. We signal our intent for an aggressive merge by riding the side of the lane market. You look at people's faces to gaze intention and attention. And when the traffic lights are down or the road is blocked by falling trees, we create impromptu order where chaos exists, nodding or waving to signal that it's someone else's term.

This was always going to be the hard part for robotaxis. That's why the same recall applies to another troubled behavioral pattern for Waymos: They struggle when officers or city workers are manually controlling and intersection. Whether it's due to a high-traffic event or an outage, it's not all that uncommon to see a police officer directing traffic by hand. They wave you through or hold you back.

But what happens if the car loses sight of the person directing traffic? What if the person directing traffic isn't actually a police officer, and waves you through a red light? What if the alternate route the police point you to spits the robotaxi onto a highway, where it isn't allowed to go?

Sources indicate that there are a million more what-ifs related to this social component of driving. All of them will have to be encountered and solved as they come, just as you and I eventually figured these things out. Recall by recall, we'll turn these Waymos into upstanding citizens.

Arknights: Endfield developer Gryphline has a good reason to celebrate, as the upcoming free-to-play action RPG has achieved yet another milestone. The developer revealed today that Endfield already has over 35 million pre-registrations.

This a major moment for the game, which is poised to be one of 2026’s biggest releases on mobile.

In December, when Gryphline officially revealed the Arknights: Endfield release date, the developer said at the time that the game had surpassed 30 million pre-registrations, meaning over 5 million more have joined in since then.

Arknights: Endfield has pretty much wrapped up closed testing, and we’re in the final stretch ahead of the January 22 launch, when the free-to-play game will go live across PC (where it'll be available via the Epic Games Store, as well as Gryphline's own launcher), PS5, and mobile platforms (iOS, Android).

In a recent development, the developer hosted a livestream to celebrate, where it also debuted two upcoming trailers: the launch trailer (below), as well as another look at gameplay. The gameplay trailer also shows off more of the game’s Talos-2 world, and sets up the mystery at the centre of its narrative.

If you’re going to be playing Endfield on PC, you’ll be happy to know that you can expert a breezy experience with support for 120fps. The game also comes with a wide range of modern technologies, including Nvidia DLSS Super Resolution, and Frame Generation. Both Xbox and PlayStation controllers are supported, too.

You can expect more Arknights: Endfield coverage from us at release and beyond. In fact, based on what we played so far, we’re pretty confident in this early Arknights Endfield characters list.

Industry News: Mysterious volcanic rock discovered in the Mariana Trench

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown.
  • That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study.
  • Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that space exploration tends to suck up most of the oxygen when it comes to venturing out into the unknown. But there’s an arguably even more mysterious frontier hidden beneath us. Nowhere is that more real than at Challenger Deep. The deepest known point on Earth, Challenger Deep is located in the 1,580-mile-long Mariana Trench at the floor of the Pacific Ocean. Getting to the bottom of this ancient chasm means diving more than 6.8 miles (around 36,000 feet) underwater. For a sense of scale, Mount Everest could be dropped into this chasm, and its summit still wouldn’t reach the surface.

That absurd depth and bone-crushing pressure make Challenger Deep brutally difficult to study. As a result, assumptions about what lies down there rarely hold up for long. Scientists long believed the area’s frigid, pitch-dark depths couldn’t sustain life, until a pair of divers reported animals near the seafloor in 1960. Now, a team using a robotic submersible in the trench says they have found the deepest evidence of explosive volcanic eruptions ever documented in the ocean.

Using the remotely operated Jason/Medea submarine robot, the team documented evidence of pyroclastic rocks (the shattered debris of violent eruptions) on the trench wall some 20,000 feet below the surface. Finding those kinds of rocks there was unexpected and will change the way geologists view the area. Writing today in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, the researchers say their discoveries may also “help explain why the Challenger Deep is so deep.”.

According to recent reports, “Explosive volcanism near trenches is unusual, so we were very surprised,” Dr. Robert J. Stern, a geologist at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author, said in a statement. “These are the deepest pyroclastic rocks documented to date from anywhere in the ocean.”.

Reaching the depth needed to study the Mariana Trench takes some serious equipment and preparation. In 2012, Titanic director James Cameron famously made the dive with a specially designed submersible that reportedly cost around $10 million to build. In this case, the team of scientists turned to a veteran robotic system called Jason/Medea. Part of the National Deep Submergence Facility and funded by the National Science Foundation, Jason/Medea traces its earliest version back to 1988. From the outside, the ROV somewhat resembles a Zamboni machine used to surface ice skating rinks.

Industry observers note that the robot can operate as deep as 21,385 feet below the surface, thanks to a roughly six-mile long fiber-optic cable connecting it to a vessel on the surface. Jason is equipped with a video and still-imaging systems. Its footage travels up through Medea, a companion robot that  hangs slightly higher in the water to buffer Jason from the motion of the vessel above. In addition to taking photos and videos, Jason has mechanical arms he can use to collect rock and sediment samples. The robotic duo has completed hundreds of dives around the world, analyzing hydrothermal vents in the Atlantic and Pacific Ocean, and even visiting a 1,600-year-old sunken Roman trading ship.

It has been revealed that in this case, the scientists deployed their robot companion in late 2024 along a 341 mile segment of the trench near Challenger Deep. Over seven dives, the robot team covered around 186 miles, taking photos and videos along the way. Analyzing the footage, the human team determined that the eastern part of the stretch is deeper than the western part and has steeper trench walls. They came across the old volcanic rocks on that steeper western side, seen below arranged in a thin flat layer. Exactly where these rocks erupted from remains unclear.

”We haven’t identified the eruption sites yet,” Stern added. “We know that these hot pyroclastic flows moved down slopes, but we don’t think they moved very far. They retained enough heat to re-weld themselves into pretty hard rocks, and that heat would’ve been lost if the pyroclastic flows traveled great distances.”.

The unexpected rocks were only one part of the expedition. The team also set out to study fragments of older, exposed crust and mantle. They also tasked the robot with studying the Shinaki Seep Field, one of deepest known hydrothermal vents sites on the planet. There was some cleanup duty as well:  the team recovered fluid-sampling devices left behind by a previous group of Japanese scientists in 2016. Explorers have rather glibly documented human trash all the way down at the bottom of Challenger Deep but these scientists, at least, won’t be adding to the litter.

#86600. 'So No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way'

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (743 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

'So No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way'

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • Showing up for friends on their good days is easy.
  • Sources indicate that this month, Marsha Linehan, developer of DBT, died.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 24, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

Showing up for friends on their good days is easy. You can celebrate their wins and enjoy their happiness. But being there, really being present for friends when they’re having a rough day or when they do dumb things, that can be more challenging. Our friend is upset, so they spend too much money, or they’re worried, so they pull out of something they had to do, or they’re angry, so they break things. How do we validate their emotions without endorsing their choices?

So, No One Told You Life Was Gonna Be This Way.

Sources indicate that this month, Marsha Linehan, developer of DBT, died. One of her many contributions to the psychology world was how to validate emotions with precision. She described six levels of how to validate emotions. The aim is to validate with the highest level possible, but different situations will require different levels. At all times, the goal is to help people notice that their emotion is valid and welcome, even if you don’t agree with the behavior that follows. Your friend doesn’t need a lecture after they’ve done something wrong; they want to feel emotionally understood.

Recent findings suggest that the most basic level is to simply stay awake and pay attention. I say "simply," but in these days of constant distractions, and phones and devices trying to hold our focus, even just being fully present can be a challenge. How can you show your friend that you’re really listening? You can use eye contact, nodding, asking questions, saying "uh-huh," and more.

The second level is accurate reflection. When you paraphrase back what they’ve remarked, you let them know that you’ve understood what they’re saying, especially the emotion they’re trying to communicate. Do this without criticism or advice, even if you don’t agree with everything they’ve said. Validation isn’t approval of behavior; it’s letting them know that their feelings are welcome.

Level three is reflecting the unarticulated parts. Let them know that you’ve understood even the aspects they haven’t explicitly told you. Name emotions that you’re guessing they’re probably feeling, e.g., "Oh my gosh, you must have been so hurt by him saying that." It doesn’t even matter if you guess the right emotion. If they reply, "Actually, I was more angry than sad," then you still have lots of emotion to validate.

At the fourth level, you are validating using past history or biology. Letting your friend know that their behavior makes sense based on their life so far. Statements like "After all you’ve been through this year, I get why this would feel so painful" can put context to their uncomfortable emotions. Even if you would have felt differently in the same situation, you are able to validate their emotion because you understand that their road to this point has been different from yours.

Even more powerful than that is normalising the emotion. Letting your friend know that anyone in that situation would probably feel the same way. Saying things like "I get so upset when that happens," or "That’s something that worries me too," or "We all have moments like that." We can normalise the emotion, even when the behavior wasn’t something we agree with. We can understand that when we’re upset, we make choices that aren’t always the most helpful, and the emotion is still valid. Also, you can normalize their emotion without launching into your own similar story; if your friend is upset, they need you to listen to their pain.

Finally, the highest level of validation is radical genuineness. You listen to them describe their experiences, and you respond with genuine emotion. You're not patronising and saying "there, there." Instead, you are moved by their situation, and you care about them. This is demonstrated through words, body language, and emotion.

Validating your friends (or partner or family member) with the highest level of validation that feels appropriate for the situation is what will help you wholeheartedly be there for them when they’re broke, their job’s a joke, or their love life’s DOA.

Koerner, K. (2012). Doing dialectical behavior therapy: A practical guide. The Guilford Press.

Linehan, M. M. (1993). Cognitive-behavioral treatment of borderline personality disorder. Guilford Press.

Linehan, M. M. (2020). Building a life worth living: A memoir. Random House.

#86599. The Porsche 718 Boxster EV Does a Convincing Impression of a Sports Car

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1610 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Roadandtrack ↗ Open Full Page

The Porsche 718 Boxster EV Does a Convincing Impression of a Sports Car

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the most vital detail about the electric Porsche 718 Boxster isn’t that it’s an EV, it’s that it’s a Porsche sports car.
  • As antithetical as an EV might be to the point of a Boxster, this 718 looks, dances, and even sounds (on the inside) like the flat-six-powered machine we’ve known and loved for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that where Porsche put the 800-volt battery pack in the Boxster flips the “every EV drives the same” trope on its side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the most vital detail about the electric Porsche 718 Boxster isn’t that it’s an EV, it’s that it’s a Porsche sports car. The new electric sports car will be officially unveiled next month, but before then, Porsche is offering up a few details on a black-and-red-camoed platter. More important, beyond the limited intel, I got to spin laps in a prototype at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles. I also rode shotgun while an engineer hotfooted it through the Angeles National Forest.

I won’t keep you in suspense. As antithetical as an EV might be to the point of a Boxster, this 718 looks, dances, and even sounds (on the inside) like the flat-six-powered machine we’ve known and loved for years. What Porsche put together is an electric car that tries harder than any before at copying the experience of a mid-engine sports car. And there’s a lot more to it than just fake noises.

Recent findings suggest that where Porsche put the 800-volt battery pack in the Boxster flips the “every EV drives the same” trope on its side. Instead of the industry-standard floor-positioned battery pack, the 718 stuffs it exactly where the internal-combustion engine was traditionally housed in the Boxster: right behind the driver’s head. This changes the weight balance from the EV-typical 50/50 to a much more mid-engine-sports-car-like 40/60. The car’s polar moment of inertia is undeniably behind you, a new sensation in the world of electric cars. Maserati planned something similar for the MC20 Folgore but canceled that project before it made production.

It has been revealed that other substantial benefits come with this battery arrangement. Engineers have been able to position the seats just as low in the floor as in the gas-powered Boxster, maintaining a proper sports-car driving position. I can promise nobody will be begging for it to be lower. It helps the design too. While this prototype was covered in camouflage, it was evident that there wasn’t a thick battery pack ruining the Boxster’s proportions. Also unaffected by the transition to electric power are the Boxster trunk and frunk. Just by eyeballing them I could tell that they look to be nearly identical to the previous car in terms of capaciousness.

Deciding how large the battery pack should be was one of the biggest problems Porsche had to solve. We’ll need to wait for the reveal to know the car’s range and battery capacity, but everything is a trade-off when it comes to an electric sports car. All we know about its curb weight is that an “intelligent lightweight construction” will yield a vehicle weight “similar to current 911 models.”.

For reference, a 911 GTS Cabriolet currently comes in around 3700 pounds. After many, many laps around the Porsche Experience Center, my gut tells me the Boxster weighs somewhere in the 3700–4000-pound range. Or, in other words, exceptional for an EV. And not so great compared with the outgoing 718 GTS 4.0, which managed to weigh in under 3200 pounds.

In a recent development, without range figures to go by, my only reference point for expectations was that the car flashed a “be mindful of range” warning after about 40 minutes of push laps on Porsche’s track. There are plenty of gas-powered sports cars that would be needing a fresh tank at that point too, although obviously not 911s equipped with the extended-range fuel tank.

Sources indicate that audible entertainment is handled by Porsche’s E-Shift system, which will come standard. This virtual simulation of a PDK transmission and engine noise debuted in the Taycan, and the new Boxster is equipped with its own version of the software. Press the button on the steering wheel, and the naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster GTS springs to life over speakers both inside and outside the car.

Recent findings suggest that engineers painstakingly measured, recorded, and reproduced the sound, then emulated a seven-speed PDK for you to shift through. Unlike the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N or the Genesis GV60 Magma, Porsche does not simulate a gas engine’s torque curve in E-Shift, preferring to maximize performance over experience. That stated, there are still some theatrics to be found. Downshifting supports “engine” braking via electric-motor regen, and you even hear the “exhaust” popping and crackling on the overrun.

Sources indicate that for many Porsche enthusiasts, it won’t be enough, especially when you remove the roof. The speakers are smart in that Porsche is able to simulate the noise as though it’s coming from behind you in traditional mid-engine fashion. But the spell is easily broken when the wind overpowers the speakers, or you gun it past a wall and there’s no delicious mechanical flat-six howl echoing back at you. It’s fake. I could tell straightaway. And everyone else will too.

Sources indicate that but alas! I had exponentially more fun driving the Boxster with E-Shift than without, especially on the track. You can choose between manual and automatic gearchanges, and I largely left it in automatic. Hearing and remembering where the “engine” revved as I approached the braking zone helped me learn the track quickly and pick out my braking points by sound alone, very similar to Road & Track’s first experience in the BMW M3 EV prototype running a comparable system.

In a recent development, then on corner exit, it supplied a faithful throttle reference that helped me trace little slides out of tighter turns in the permissive PSM Sport traction mode. As soon as I turned E-Shift off, I felt lost on the track. And call me old-fashioned, but silently skittering between corners with just the sound of tire squeal is sad. Even more so, because this chassis is a damn good one.

It has been revealed that porsche is being coy with the finer details but let on that numerous chassis components are based on those found in the 911. Boxster owners will be familiar with this hand-me-down strategy, and it continues into the electric era. The steering, braking system, and wheel-and-tire combinations are based on the 911. Pirelli P Zero R summer tires were fitted to staggered wheels (20s in front and 21s in rear) for my time in the car, with a 255-section width in front and a 305-section width in the rear. The new car has PASM damping tech, and engineers note both the damper and spring calibration are softer than those in an equivalent 911. The suspension’s controlled but comfortable composure over rough sections of the road confirmed as much. Thankfully, the brakes just felt like brakes with no weird regen sensation and plenty of feel at the limit.

My test car didn’t have it, but a sport suspension will also be available. And for the first time, the 718 gets optional rear-axle steering, not to help tighten its turning radius but to supply greater stability at high speeds where the rear wheels can turn in coordination with the fronts. There’s even a front-axle lift, picking up where the Spyder RS left off as the first Boxster with stated feature.

Recent findings suggest that the powertrain itself is all good news. Porsche wouldn’t supply an output number, but the car I drove employs a single electric motor in the rear. It’s reportedly powerful enough for a 0–60-mph run in under three seconds. Porsche says it will be the most powerful 718 so far, meaning more than the 493-hp output of the GT4 RS, and it will almost certainly be the quickest to 60 too. As with Porsche’s other EVs, there’s a push-to-pass mode you can activate for 10 seconds at a time, and using launch control unleashes maximum output too. But at no point was I wanting for more punch around the relatively tight track. Once the tires warmed, launching was effortless, and I didn’t doubt the sub-three-second claim for a moment. The same goes for the road drive, where the Boxster is powerful enough to need serious restraint to not end up doing jail speeds.

Porsche Torque Vectoring Plus, another feature derived from the 911, helps dole out power between the two rear wheels to maximum effectiveness. Between this power-distribution system and the Boxster’s happy tendency to kindly bend itself into corners under braking, this 718 has the balance and more jovial nature of the previous one. But another trait carries over: The rear indicates a tendency to dance further out than you would expect from an EV with a more typical 50/50 weight distribution. And despite that Porsche puts massive emphasis on keeping weight down (it even reduced the charge ports from its typical two to only one), there was no denying that this Boxster felt porkier than before. The difference was most obvious in the tighter corners where the mass couldn’t be disguised and the grippy front tires ultimately surrendered to the sheer weight that is being asked to turn.

Porsche notes it will be launching the electric Boxster into the world with two versions to start. While it wouldn’t reveal the trims, I do know that the version I drove will be the spicier of the two, therefore corresponding with the previous Boxster S. I can’t be certain whether it’s a hit or a miss until I experience the final production car, but I can say this is much more than simply an electric powertrain transplant.

Recent findings suggest that it challenges the hard-core among us in ways EVs simply haven’t before, and if it’s not your cup of tea, don’t worry. Porsche will keep making gas-powered performance cars. It’s just a shame that they won’t start under $100,000, where this one is projected to begin.

Tesla FSD V15 Makes Your Drive Look Like Grand Theft Auto

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s latest version of Full Self-Driving lets you swing a virtual camera around your car like you’re cruising through Leonida in Grand Theft Auto.
  • The feature is called Tesla Reality View, and it’s reaching early-access users with FSD V15.
  • The manufacturer says this fresh FSD version is 25 times safer when it does critical interventions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s latest version of Full Self-Driving lets you swing a virtual camera around your car like you’re cruising through Leonida in Grand Theft Auto. It’s a neat trick, especially when you consider that the Tesla has to generate the scenery as it goes. It also gets a little floating arrow, which now lets you know which roundabout exit it’s going to take.

The feature is called Tesla Reality View, and it’s reaching early-access users with FSD V15. The earlier parking display drew outlines of nearby objects, but this one recreates the street around you in real time and shows where FSD intends to turn or park. You can have this on the whole screen, split it with the map, or let the map take over instead. There’s also a quieter cabin mode, and even the turn signal sound fades after a few clicks.

The manufacturer says this fresh FSD version is 25 times safer when it does critical interventions. The upgrade to the software that interprets camera images was trained on millions of internet videos and shared with its Robotaxi and Optimus programs. What’s not clear is the starting figure. How many miles did the previous version go between critical interventions, and under what conditions? Tesla doesn’t say.

Recent findings suggest that will drivers actually notice? Tesla notes V15 is better at spotting potholes, small animals, signs, and debris, including chains (which have been known to cause crashes and have drawn federal scrutiny). It should also avoid deep standing water and choose more appropriate speeds in school zones and bad weather.

Sources indicate that tesla indicates the navigation now learns from the routes other Teslas actually take, initially at the start and end of a trip. Tesla aims to extend that approach to the whole route later. Once you arrive, the map can show several parking options, and FSD uses your parking history to help pick one. It’s another application of the fleet learning feature Tesla demonstrated with V12.

V15 can also slow for a speed camera, but if you override it twice for the same camera, the car will remember your preference. Bike Rack Mode lets FSD operate with a rack on the tow hitch, though it won’t automatically reverse for you at the destination, leaving parking up to you. Autopark, Summon and backup warnings are disabled in that mode.

Industry observers note that in a roughly 25-minute drive, Sawyer Merritt found V15 more cautious around pedestrians than V14. In one parking lot, he remarked the car braked for someone running across its path before he spotted them himself.

While parking, Merritt could see which space FSD had picked, but tapping another space did nothing. He had to switch to manual, select the spot, and reengage FSD. It then parked where he wanted. That parking maneuver makes a pretty good case for the GTA graphics, which now give you a much better idea of what’s around the car and what it’s about to do, but the 25-fold safety improvement claim will need more than a drive to Best Buy to judge.
